processes: Passing vibrations through the middle ear
Turning vibrations into signals in the cochlea
plainLanguageExplanation: The ear has three main parts. The outer ear (the visible part plus the ear canal) funnels sound waves toward the eardrum. The middle ear has three tiny bones (hammer, anvil, stirrup) that pass the vibrations on and make them stronger. The inner ear contains the coiled cochlea, which turns the vibrations into nerve signals, and the semicircular canals, which help with balance. The signals from the cochlea travel along the auditory nerve to the brain, which turns them into the sounds you recognize. So hearing is a chain: sound waves, vibrations, signals, brain.

whyItMatters: The ear lets you hear sounds and keep your balance. Understanding it explains how loud noises can damage hearing, why your ears pop, and how a tiny chain of bones passes vibrations from the air to your brain.
tagline: The organ of hearing and balance
didYouKnow: Your eardrum is only about 0.1 mm thick, yet it can be set vibrating by a sound and pass those vibrations to three of the body's tiniest bones.
